explanations.answer: The LORD will rule over you
explanations.explanation: Gideon, Israel's leader in the fight with Midian, hears the offer: rule over us, you, your son and your grandson. He says, “I will not rule over you, nor will my son. The LORD shall rule over you.” (Judges 8:23) That's the answer, baker. Offered a crown, and he hands it right back. Meanwhile I can't even turn down the last cookie on the cooling rack.

explanations.answer: My son will rule in my place
explanations.explanation: Gideon says the opposite. His words are “I will not rule over you, nor will my son.” The son gets turned down along with the father. The throne goes back on the shelf.

explanations.answer: I will rule until Midian is gone
explanations.explanation: There's no short-term contract in his answer. Gideon says, “I will not rule over you…” and he says it flat out. The people offered rule to him, his son and his grandson. He answered that the LORD shall rule over them.

Gideon asks, and the Israelites answer, “We will give them gladly…” Then they spread out a garment, and each man throws an earring from his plunder onto it. Gladly, friend. I've seen people hold onto a cookie harder than that, and I was one of them.

The text says the opposite. When Gideon asks for the earrings, the Israelites reply, “We will give them gladly…” So they spread out a garment, and each man throws an earring onto it. Nobody grumbles in this passage.

Gideon placed the ephod in Ophrah, his hometown. Hold on to that spot, friend, because the very next words tell us what happened there. The verse says all Israel worshiped it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and his household. (Judges 8:27)

Shiloh, baker? I love the confidence. You said it like you had directions in your hand. The text puts the ephod in Ophrah, Gideon's hometown (Judges 8:27), and Shiloh never shows up in this passage. I once spent a whole afternoon sure I'd left my timer in one spot, and it was in my apron the entire time.

Bethel! Another good one, friend, but nobody in this passage is packing a bag for Bethel. Gideon keeps the ephod close to home, in Ophrah, his hometown. (Judges 8:27) Nobody had to travel far to find it, and that's the part that stings, because Israel ended up worshiping it right there.

The text says the ephod “…became a snare to Gideon and his household.” A snare is a trap that catches you. All Israel ended up worshiping it there, and that's the trouble. Sometimes the thing that grabs your ankle is the one nobody saw coming.
A shield protects, and this did the opposite. The verse says the ephod became a snare to Gideon and his household. All Israel was worshiping it there. That's a trap, not a shield.

That would be a happy ending, and the verse doesn't give one. It says the ephod “…became a snare to Gideon and his household.” The people worshiping it is exactly what the text says went wrong. I wish it said blessing, friend, but it doesn't.

The text says, “So the land had rest for forty years in the days of Gideon…” Midian was subdued and never raised its head again. That's forty years with no Midian at the door. Forty years of rest is longer than I've ever gone without burning at least one batch.
The verse says the opposite. Midian was subdued and did not raise its head again, so “…the land had rest for forty years in the days of Gideon…” The fighting was over. It was a long stretch of quiet.
No famine in this verse. It says Midian was subdued, and “…the land had rest for forty years in the days of Gideon…” Forty quiet years followed the fight. Rest is the word the text uses.

The text says, “Gideon had seventy sons of his own, since he had many wives.” Seventy sons is a lot of birthdays. That's a lot of names to remember, and I'm the guy who forgets which drawer he put the spatula in. Hold on to this number, because those sons come up again.

The text doesn't say that. It says Gideon had seventy sons “…of his own, since he had many wives.” Those are his own sons, and the verse gives the reason right there. Boys from Midian never come up in it.

Nice try, friend, but his brothers' sons never show up in this verse. It says Gideon had seventy sons “…of his own, since he had many wives.” His own sons, and the verse hands us the reason. Seventy of them. I can barely keep track of one batch of cookies.
The text says, “…Gideon son of Joash died at a ripe old age…” He was buried in the tomb of his father Joash in Ophrah of the Abiezrites. A long life, and he's buried in his father's tomb.

explanations.answer: In the middle of his life
explanations.explanation: The text puts it later than that. It says Gideon “…died at a ripe old age…” He wasn't cut off in his prime. He had a long life behind him when he was buried in his father Joash's tomb.
Not young at all. The verse says Gideon “…died at a ripe old age…” He was buried in the tomb of his father Joash in Ophrah. That's a lot of birthdays behind him.

The text says, “…as soon as Gideon was dead, the Israelites turned and prostituted themselves with the Baals…” The Baals were false gods. “…as soon as…” is the part that stings. Earlier the Israelites offered Gideon rule, and the moment he was gone they turned to the Baals.

The text never says that. It says that as soon as Gideon was dead, “…the Israelites turned and prostituted themselves with the Baals…” The Baals were false gods, and the people went after them. Nobody grabs a furnace in this verse.

That's not what the verse says. It says that as soon as Gideon was dead, “…the Israelites turned and prostituted themselves with the Baals…” Verse 35 adds that they did not show kindness to the house of Jerubbaal. The passage never records anyone asking his sons to lead.

The verse says, “The Israelites failed to remember the LORD their God who had delivered them from the hands of all their enemies on every side.” He had delivered them, and they didn't remember it. It's like forgetting who baked the batch while you're eating the cookies. Friend, that's a hard thing to read.

The text says the Israelites “…failed to remember the LORD their God who had delivered them from the hands of all their enemies on every side.” They did fail. He had delivered them, and they didn't remember Him. It's a sad line.

The text says the opposite. “They did not show kindness to the house of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) for all the good things he had done for Israel.” Gideon had done good things for Israel, and his house got no kindness back. I think that one stings.

The verse says, “They did not show kindness to the house of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) for all the good things he had done for Israel.” Jerubbaal is Gideon's other name. After all the good he did for them, his house got no kindness. I think that one hurts.
